name: The Champion Basswood of Busse Forest South

location.address: Busse Forest South, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
story:
This is the biggest basswood on all the land of the Forest Preserves of Cook County, first in their champion tree register. Its trunk is 3.91 metres round, and it stands 24.4 metres tall under a crown about 16 metres one way and 17 the other.

The same preserve holds the county's third-ranked basswood, about 730 metres to the north, and the two are an instructive pair. They are exactly the same height, 24.4 metres each. The difference is all in the trunk: this one is 80 centimetres thicker round, and the register ranks it first and the other third. Stand at one and then the other, and you are looking at the same species, the same height and the same woods, with the champion simply carrying more wood.

Busse Forest South holds a third ranked tree as well, the county's second-ranked sugar maple, about two and a half kilometres to the east and twelve metres taller than either basswood. Together they make a long walk past three trees the county has measured and ranked.

The register records the size and place but no measurement date, and nothing about age. Nobody has dated this basswood. If you know how old it is, or when it was last measured, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 3.91 metres round, the thicker of the two ranked basswoods in Busse Forest South. It stands about 730 metres south of the third-ranked one, at the register's point.

name: The Third-Ranked Basswood of Busse Forest South

location.address: Busse Forest South, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
story:
This basswood is the third biggest the Forest Preserves of Cook County have measured on their land, and it stands just 730 metres from the champion. The two are exactly the same height, 24.4 metres each.

Where they part is the trunk. This one is 3.11 metres round against the champion's 3.91. Its crown, though, is the wider of the two, about 19 metres one way and 16 the other, so from a distance it may look the larger tree. Up close, the trunk tells them apart, and the register ranks this one third.

That makes Busse Forest South a good place to train your eye. Walk between the two basswoods and you see how much a species can vary in one woodland: same height, same ground, eighty centimetres of trunk between them. The preserve's other ranked tree, the county's second-ranked sugar maple, stands about two and a half kilometres to the southeast and rises to 36.6 metres, half as tall again as either basswood.

The register records size and place but no date of measurement and no age. Nobody has dated this tree. If you know how old it is, or have measured it yourself, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wide crown, about 19 by 16 metres, over a trunk 3.11 metres round, slimmer than the champion's. It stands about 730 metres north of the champion basswood.

name: The Pin Oak of Rolling Knolls

location.address: Rolling Knolls, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
story:
This pin oak's crown spreads about 26 metres one way and 22 the other, on a tree only 29 metres tall. It is the champion pin oak of the Forest Preserves of Cook County, first among all those on preserve land, and it is nearly as wide as it is high.

The trunk is 3.59 metres round. Put the tree beside the county's champion white oak at Red Gate Woods, itself notable for a broad, even crown: that oak is 29.3 metres tall, almost the same, yet its crown is about three metres narrower across its widest line. No crown among the Cook County champions on our Chicago page spreads further than this one.

Pin oaks are familiar on our map from the other side of the Atlantic. We list them in Dutch parks in Haarlem, Apeldoorn, Eindhoven and Sittard, where the registers record planting dates between the 1860s and about 1910. None of those carries a measured trunk or crown on our pages, so this champion is the first pin oak we can describe in numbers.

Rolling Knolls lies at the far western edge of the trees on this page, a trip of its own rather than part of a walk.

The register records no measurement date and no age. Nobody has dated this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 26 by 22 metres, nearly as wide as the 29-metre tree is tall, over a trunk 3.59 metres round. It stands at the register's point in Rolling Knolls.

name: The Cottonwood of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Entrance on Chicago Ave, west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest, IL 60305, Forest Preserves of Cook County

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, record 45

access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/thatcher-woods/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
transport: Entrance Chicago Ave west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest; public transport not verified.
story:
At 41.5 metres, this cottonwood is the tallest tree anyone has measured on our Chicago map, and the Forest Preserves of Cook County still rank it only second among their cottonwoods.

The trunk is just as far out of scale. Measured in July 2023, it is 5.94 metres round, the thickest recorded girth on this page. The crown is far from round: about 28 metres one way and only 17 the other. Somewhere else on preserve land stands a cottonwood the register puts ahead of it.

It also anchors the best short walk on the page. About 130 metres to the north stands the county's second-ranked silver maple, and just beyond it the two ranked hackberries, the champion and its taller runner-up. A third-ranked bitternut hickory stands about 400 metres to the south-east. That is five register trees inside roughly 600 metres of the same woods.

The nearest rival in size is another cottonwood, at National Grove about seven kilometres south: 5.82 metres round, 39 metres tall, and ranked third.

Everything here comes from one source, the county's champion tree register, which records size, rank and place. It says nothing about age. Nobody has dated this cottonwood. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 41.5 metres tall on a trunk 5.94 metres round, the biggest of the ranked trees in Thatcher Woods. It stands about 130 metres south of the second-ranked silver maple.

name: The Second-Ranked Hackberry of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Entrance on Chicago Ave, west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest, IL 60305, Forest Preserves of Cook County

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, record 307

access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/thatcher-woods/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
transport: Entrance Chicago Ave west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest; public transport not verified.
story:
This hackberry stands 2.4 metres taller than the county's champion hackberry, 66 metres away, and the register still ranks it second.

At 39 metres, 128 feet, it is the tallest of the three hackberries at the top of the Forest Preserves of Cook County's champion register. The champion beats it everywhere else: 3.51 metres round against this tree's 3.35, and a crown about 22 metres across both ways against this one's 19.5 by 15.5. The register crowns the stout tree, not the tall one.

For a sense of what 39 metres means for the species, the only other common hackberry we have measured, the Leaning Hackberry of Parco Treves in Padua, is 9 metres tall. This one is more than four times that.

The pair is the reason to come. Stand between them and you see one species on one patch of ground grown two ways, one taller and one stouter. The county's second-ranked silver maple stands about 30 metres to the south, and the second-ranked cottonwood, at 41.5 metres the one ranked tree here taller still, about 160 metres south.

The register gives no date for this measurement and no age. It is the only source for the tree. Nobody has dated this hackberry. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 39 metres, taller and slimmer than the champion hackberry 66 metres away. It stands about 30 metres north of the second-ranked silver maple.

name: The Bitternut Hickory of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Entrance on Chicago Ave, west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest, IL 60305, Forest Preserves of Cook County

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, record 20

access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/thatcher-woods/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
transport: Entrance Chicago Ave west of Thatcher Ave, River Forest; public transport not verified.
story:
This bitternut hickory stands 34 metres tall on a trunk only 1.92 metres round, about 61 centimetres across.

That is a lot of tree on a slim stem. The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it in November 2023 and ranked it third among the bitternut hickories on their land. Its height, 34.1 metres, matches the third-ranked hackberry at National Grove to the decimetre, on a trunk little more than half that tree's girth.

Bitternut is a tree we rarely get to show. The only other one on our map grows in Ottawa's Dominion Arboretum, where it was planted between 1886 and 1890 and no girth is recorded. This one has measurements and no history; that one has history and no measurements.

In Thatcher Woods it sits at the south-east end of the preserve's ranked trees: about 400 metres from the second-ranked cottonwood and about 580 metres from the champion hackberry. Walk the group from north to south and the hickory is where you finish.

The county's champion register is the only source for it. It records size, rank and the measurement date, and nothing on age. Nobody has dated this hickory. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the slender trunk, 1.92 metres round, on a tree 34 metres tall. It stands about 400 metres south-east of the second-ranked cottonwood, the southernmost of the ranked trees in Thatcher Woods.

name: The Chinkapin Oak of National Grove

location.address: National Grove North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside, IL 60546, Forest Preserves of Cook County

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, record 230

access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/national-grove/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
transport: North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside; public transport not verified.
story:
This is the only chinkapin oak on our map, and it happens to be the biggest one the Forest Preserves of Cook County have found on all their land.

The county measured it in July 2024 and ranked it first of its species in their champion tree register. Its trunk is 3.72 metres round, and it stands 29.3 metres tall, exactly the height of the county's champion white oak at Red Gate Woods. Its crown spreads about 25 metres one way and 23 the other, close to round, a fraction narrower than the champion pin oak's at Rolling Knolls.

The point of coming to National Grove is that it does not stand alone. About 240 metres to the south is the county's third-ranked hackberry, and about 125 metres beyond that the third-ranked cottonwood, 5.82 metres round and 39 metres tall. Three ranked trees of three different species in under 400 metres make this the second walk on the page, after Thatcher Woods to the north.

Of those three, the oak is the only champion. That title is about size on preserve land, not age, and the register keeps no age for any of its trees. It is also the only source for this one. Nobody has dated this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only oak among National Grove's ranked trees, a trunk 3.72 metres round under a crown about 25 by 23 metres. It stands about 240 metres north of the third-ranked hackberry.

name: The Cottonwood of National Grove

location.address: National Grove North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside, IL 60546, Forest Preserves of Cook County

official_register.name: Forest Preserves of Cook County Champion Tree Register, record 47

access: Free. Forest Preserves of Cook County: open year-round, sunrise to sunset (preserve page: fpdcc.com/places/locations/national-grove/, read via Wayback 2025 copy).
transport: North entrance W 26th St east of 1st Ave, North Riverside; public transport not verified.
story:
Ranked only third among Cook County's forest preserve cottonwoods, this tree has a trunk 5.82 metres round, the thickest recorded on our Chicago map bar one.

The exception is its rival at Thatcher Woods, about seven kilometres north. The two are close enough to be twins on paper: 12 centimetres of girth and 2.5 metres of height between them, this one at 39 metres, 128 feet, and the Thatcher tree at 41.5. The register still sets a full ranked place between them.

To see how far out of line these cottonwoods are, set this one beside the oaks. The thickest white oak on this page, the county's second-ranked tree at McClaughrey Springs Woods, is 4.76 metres round, more than a metre thinner. The champion chinkapin oak a few hundred metres north of here manages 3.72.

The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it on 21 December 2023, the same day as the third-ranked hackberry, which stands about 125 metres to the north-north-east. With the chinkapin oak beyond that, it makes the southern end of a short line of three ranked trees in National Grove.

The register is the only source for this tree, and it records size and rank but not age. Nobody has dated this cottonwood. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.82 metres round, far thicker than the hackberry nearby, on a tree 39 metres tall. It stands about 125 metres south-south-west of the third-ranked hackberry.
